sentences.text: This meeting is being recorded.
Hey, Andy.
Hi, Mark.
How you doing?
I'm doing all right.
How are you?
Yeah, I'm good, thank you.
I'm good.
Where about C calling from?
We are in Minneapolis, Minnesota.
How about you?
Wow.
I am in the uk.
I don't know how well you know it, but about an hour and a half outside London.
All right.
I mean, I am an avid Premier League fan, so like anybody else in the States, if you learn about geography elsewhere and you're a footy fan, you learn it through footy and that's it.
Okay.
Yeah, well, this.
We're not in a hot spot here in the Southwest, so unfortunately, all the good teams are up in the Northwest, but that's where I'm from, so.
Okay.
Right on.
Yeah.
Well, it's nice to meet you.
Manchester, which is your team, for better or for worse?
I'm an Arsenal fan.
I grew up watching Henri and he was a bit of an inspiration.
He's who I tried to mimic my game like, but obviously I'm in a creative field, so didn't quite have the same success.
But you, how about you?
Are you.
Are you a fan?
Do you watch?
Not much of a fan, actually, but my wife used to be in business with Thierry Henry's wife, so we do have.
Oh, really?
Yes.
Well, ex wife, should I say?
They had a laundry business together.
Small world.
Yeah, it is a small world, but Arsenal is the.
Is the other one.
We're from.
We are Londoners from North London.
So Arsenal's the.
The local ground.
All right.
That's kind of.
I mean, recently.
Not a bad team to be.
To be supporting, but a little bit of a rocky patch since Banger's departure.
Yeah.
Anyway, getting better.
Yeah.
Well, good to know you're somewhat of an Anglophile, at least through the footy, so that's all good.
Exactly.
So, yeah.
Well, thank you for getting in touch.
So I'll be interested to learn a little bit more about you.
I don't know what you know about us.
Obviously you're on our mailing list, which is great, but we are Capital A, so we're an M and A advisory for marketing services companies.
So all of our clients are either buy or sell side, but the buyers tend to be either high growth agencies or private equity or private investors.
On the sell side as well, we've got the Platform Agencies Co, which is our marketplace for buyers and sellers of agencies.
So we work both the buy and the sell side.

You were interested in the roll up, so I'll be keen to sort of get to to know what it is that exactly you're looking for because we are building our own roll up at the moment which you may know from our newsletter or whether it's just yeah.
You're looking to to be part of a roll up or build your own roll up as well.
Which is always a a good place to to shoot for if you're planning on exiting at a better multiple.
Yeah.
So a little I appreciate the background and obviously part of your mailing list and just get the, the news that you guys are putting out there, which is super helpful.
And and I'll tell you a little bit about me, a little bit about squid.
So I, I come prior to starting squid, so we're 10 years old now.
I was brand side prior to that.
I worked for an organization called Marc Anthony Group.
They are a adult beverage brand.
They're now their international headquarters is based out of Ireland, but they were Canadian with the US Headquarters in Chicago.
Launch brands like White Claw, Hard Seltzer, which I know is starting to make its way or make some headway in the uk.
That was actually Agency Squid's first project when I left.
So we do a lot in the adult beverage space and consumer packaged goods space as well as hospitality and tourism and luxury goods.
I reached out because I mean your, your email was timely.
I have a business partner.
We are a family business.
He's my dad.
He is on hit.
We're, we're talking succession planning.
The man deserves to not work.
He's, he's been a sole proprietor for 50 years and so he's going down to part time this year.
As we look at what kind of the next stage of SQUID is going to be.
When you would read when your email came through about roll ups, this is one of the things what we're exploring right now is we're a small boutique.
We didn't come from a giant holding company and take a bunch of clients with us.
Everything that we have built has been built by our hands over the last decade.

I have come to the realization, especially after last year, which was a difficult year for us after being the first year that we didn't see growth, even though we're very much back on track this year.
I don't know how closely you are following you follow the political nonsense that is happening in our country, but that does seem to kind of take a toll on some of the agencies in our, in our space.
So again, very fortunate that we're back on our growth trajectory.
But it has given me pause to think about what is the next step for squid.
And if I'm honest, going it as a sole proprietor seems like a pretty daunting task, especially for the ambition that I have for this agency.
And so there's an.
I am going through this process of exploring whether it's we dilute our equity and bring on individual partners to help us in our growth or if we roll up with like minded agencies for the.
To your.
Your original point of.
For an exit further down the line.
Again from my own personal ambition, I where I'm setting out to be and hope to be one of the best independent agencies in the country.
But I've come to the realization after a decade of some really solid wins, to do it alone is going to be difficult.
And I think that there are some people out there that like to do things that I don't like to do and that inversely I things that I like to do that they don't like to do.
I'm not a song and dance type of person.
I'm not a flashy person and there are plenty of people in my space that love that.
I love the op side of it and the people management side of it and the strategy side.
So that's, that's why when that email came to us, like I think it's at least worth the conversation.

I'm like I said, exploring what this next evolution of SKUID is and if I want to be bullish on doing something that leaves a lasting impression in the space, but also thinking about my own long term goals of eventually leaving this industry, that's kind of where I'm at.
I know that that's very broad, Andy, so apologies, but at least gives you a sense of where my head's at.
Yeah, no, that's brilliant.
Thank you.
Okay, so just a couple of questions around the business then.
So you're doing 1.5 million revenue at the moment.
Yep.
And what's your margin?
Do you know what your profit margin is on that?
I mean if I'm taking out salaries and we own the property that we.
So that's where our financials look a little odd because we own the real estate that we're renting from.
So we have a separate LLC there.
And we also reinvest our profits in two brands that we own as well.
One is tequila brand and one is a golf accessories brand, which I also know makes things a little difficult.
But I would say our profit margins are probably 30, 40%.
Most of the work that comes through here is brand and design work or things of that nature.
All of which the skill sets internal.
So are really the only, the only considerations that we have from a financial standpoint are paying off the building and our staff.
But other than that, we have really, really low overhead.
Purposefully is because I didn't want to be an agency that when you lose a client or win a client, you scale up or scale back accordingly.
So, okay, how big is your team?
How many people you've got working for you full time?
And any freelancers?
Oh, big handful of freelancers.
I would say if we're including the 1099s, we're closer to 20.
Okay.
And they're regular contractors that you're working with?
Yeah.
Okay.
And part of that is.

Yeah, I'm sure as you know, as you're talking to agencies, the way of the world, especially if you're wanting to compete and you're a small agency, the best talent really is talent that's on the street and freelancing that don't want to work in agencies anymore.
So we had to create a model that was.
Our staff is all senior.
We have no junior talent, which is very purposeful, allows us to take much bigger swings.

But because of that there's kind of this balance of the 1099 who don't want to be agency side but still want interesting work, but like I said, don't want to do the client management, don't want to do X, Y and don't want to do the financials, don't want to do all of that thing, those types of things.
So that's, that's our structure.
Okay, that makes sense.
And it's very common.
You're right.
Okay, so there's you and your dad.
What's the ownership?
Is it 50, 15.
He wants to, he wants to retire.
Yeah.
And did you say that he's been working 50 years or that the agency was 50 years.
It's 10 years old.
He's been working 50 years.
He was one foot out the door when I suckered him into this venture.
So.
But no one's, no one was going to take a 20 year old seriously.
And talking to CMOs.
Um, and also I don't have, I certainly don't have the background that he does in terms of brand building.
Cause he's an old school brand guy.

And I grew up in the digital age, so to me it was a point of differentiation where you had the two senior leaders who actually saw what integrated marketing and advertising should be like coming from two ends of the spectrum.
So it, it helped us get off the ground and get that point of differentiation and then as sense evolved to being a very strategy heavy shop with a lot of insight driven, creative.
Okay, so in terms of a rollup, what you're thinking is you would like to go into a roll up of some sort.
So obviously the idea behind a rollup is to.
Well, at least if you're being part of one.
Yeah.
Usually to lead the roll up and if you can't lead it, you would look at being a bolt on.
So there's two types of those businesses that go into those groups.
One is a platform business which is usually Fairly large, usually 1 or 2 million EBITDA at least.
And then you have the smaller businesses which are bolt ons that sit around that sort of central business.
Sure.
So it would look from your point of view very similar to being acquired.
So are you saying that there's a big difference for you personally in the idea of being in a roll up from being acquired to running your own roll up?
I mean is it, is there a differentiate between those or the only the same thing?
I think that that's a, it's a great question.
I think the reason why I would look at roll up over full acquisition is because I, I know what this business can be worth over time and I can get it there.
I just would rather not to.

And I think that if we were to be acquired now and we were based solely on revenue of the last, I mean especially with last year being as tough as it was, I don't think that we would get the valuation that would make me excited to be part of something bigger.
So that's where diluting equity I'm okay with more than okay with.

For the idea of if that roll up is a bolt on of several different shops at Acquisition further down the road, just making sure that, that those dividends kind of play out once that larger entity is looking at that next phase.

So I'm, I'm trying to, trying to be realistic and a little bit pragmatic because I know like I said, coming off of the year that we had, it's not going to financially look the way that at least maybe it's just my own ego but the where our business can be.
So that, that's my thought and I'm happy.
Again, I know nothing about this and I am a, I am a strategist and I live in this world.
That's why I'm talking to people like you.
So what I would say is in terms of a roll up, if we were to run it, we're looking for Larger companies that are doing 1 million EBITDA.
Because when you get to those metrics, for us, we get a much bigger multiple.
So I think what you're looking for is possibly either to be the target of a bolt on which.
Which is the same as being acquired.
The only real difference is you usually have a piece of equity that you roll over in the top co.
So they would roll over somewhere between 20 and 40%, they would acquire 60% and then you would all work together to build the group and then exit in three to five years.
So that is one way.
But the other thing that kind of sticks out to me is maybe something along.

More along the lines of being in a merger with another agency that's around a similar size, because that would get you kind of into the zone that you need to be a little bit bigger to get slightly better multiples when you exit.
But also finding that guy that wants to be the front man, I guess that wants to be.
Yeah, life maybe.
Right.
You can focus on the ops and between the two.
And I would say the majority of founders that I meet is the other type rather than the operational guy.
So.
So there's probably opportunity to merge with a similar sized company and maybe either one locally or that's on the other side of the country.
So it kind of makes sense for you to either win two different bits of business.
Right.
Because you're both in the same region or city that you could merge more easily.
I would say on the latter, I mean, one, I'm happy to hear that there are more people that like the song and dance than me because it's something that I really don't like.
I am not a front man at all.
I like being in the background.
If anything, I'd be the tour manager for a band that would be rocking out and having somebody else do the song and dance.
I'm totally cool with that.
I know my strengths and I know my weaknesses.
I will say for us being in the middle of the country, a majority of our clientele is not.
If you've had a chance to look at our work, we do some really weird things.
So I think having a presence in other parts of the country, if we were to be doing a merger, would make a ton of sense versus continuing to be in the Midwest.
It's not the work that we really like to do and it's.
It's very safe, it's very practical.
It's status quo.
That's just not.
That's just not our culture.

But yes, what you just explained, those two pieces is whether it's, like I said, diluting my equity, which I'm more than comfortable with if that becomes an acquisition or if it's a merger with another shop that either has, you know, similar capabilities or as a media agency that needs creative.
I don't know I am open to any of these conversations.
These are just not conversations that I've.
I've had in the past.
But yeah, okay.
So.
Well, we probably can't introduce you to all of those types of things.
The issue for us is working on a merger that.
No, no.
Money changes hands and we work on our win fees.
Right.
There wouldn't be a whole lot of upside for us, so we just don't focus on that type of work.

But we would be potentially open to do that type of work, but it would be retainer based until we found that type of business that was a good match and that you could get a deal done with the other founder.
Sure.
The other way that we could work together is we could get you listed on the agency's platform.
So there's a few tiers on there.
There's sort of a dip your toe in water where we just provide you with valuation, build all the marketing materials and get you up and listed on our site.
Obviously we've got traffic come to the site and then we've got our mailing list as well, which we would market the opportunity to.

So what usually happens is people that are kind of bit more risk averse and they don't want to invest too much, they go down that route and then we, we probably get anywhere from sort of 10 to 40 signed NDAs in the first 24 hours and we don't really have to do a ton more work to find buyers because you've already got some interest.
You have these conversations and so it's relatively low risk to you and you start those conversations and one of them might be a good match.
So that's kind of like the sort of easiest way into it.
Sure.
And then we have like a full process where we're working every single day for six months to get a deal done.
Which, which is more of an investment and more intense.
Yeah, I don't sure that that's where your, where your head is at at the moment.
These are more exploratory sort of things.
So.
So yeah, happy to, to answer any questions around those options.
I think the merger route would most likely involve you probably either reaching out to some agency owners that you already knew or were in the area and saying, you know, this is what We're.
We're thinking my dad's planning on retiring.
I'm looking for the rock star.
Right.
Yeah.
Or whatever.
Yeah.
Which would be a good place to start, you know, because everybody's looking for backing dancers and bass players.
But you know what.
What I feel like anyway, because most of the people that I speak to are the weirdos that run the agencies.
So somebody from your background.
I mean, don't get me wrong, I am a weirdo that runs an agency.
It's just different.
It looks very different than what your typical creative weirdo would look like.
My own eccentric nature is a little bit more subdued.
But hey, your.
Your cardigan is absolutely.
It's bang on, so.
Oh, thank you.
It's so Andy.
I call it grandpa casual.
That is.
That is my wardrobe in the winter and my team makes fun of me, but it's like all cardigans and, and stuff like that.
For someone that's in their late 30s.
Go for it.
But there's a.
There's a closet creative in there somewhere.
Yeah, I, I come out and play every now and again, but I let the cre.
The real creatives do the work that I just like being around them, so.
I know what you mean.
I know.
I mean, that's kind of my role.
So.
Yeah, I think, look, I can send you some stuff over and you can have a think about what kind of, you know, way forward would be the most sensible for you.
But as well, you know, I bet your dad's not in a rush to, to retire either.
He's probably.
Maybe he's the.
The creative guy and he loves what he's doing, I'm pretty sure.
So you don't, you don't want to go out on a low.
You want to make sure you're building the business to something that's going to be, you know, a great exit for.
For you.
So hopefully that's been some help.
That has for sure.
Yeah.
And get.

It will get you started anyway with these conversations and certainly we would be able to sort of take you somewhere where we would have buyers at the table who would be willing to talk about what you wanted to do in terms of selling and if we went to market, you know, with conversations.
Sorry, you froze.
I froze.
You frozen?
Yeah.
Now you're back.
All right, so we could, we could still.
I think there would be a, you know, good possibility that we could find the right types of buyers.
We would just go to the mark to market.
With your story being specific that you would.
You were looking for a majority share Share sale.
But you wanted to retain, you know, 20 or 40 of the business.
We went to market with that as the story.
Then we would attract those types of buyers and you could have those conversations and that would be your way into a roll up.
So I can send.
Awesome.
Excuse me.
I'll send you the Costa.
My God.
Got some in my throat.
So I just had some sesame seeds.
So I can send some information over about that.
And maybe.
Yeah, I mean, if there's more interest after you had a conversation with your dad or whatever, that we could.
We could go down that route and.
That would be awesome.
Yeah, anything that you have, Andy, would be really appreciative.
Like I said, this is just trying to find the next best play for the agency, what we're trying to accomplish.
And also, you know, I'm trying to think a little bit more future planning than the guy who's been in the business 50 years.
If I don't.
Honestly, I don't want to do what he did.
So if I was in your shoes, I would just do a search of agencies in your city and just reach out to them and just say, we're looking at partners for a merger.
I bet you would have a ton of really interesting conversations and it would get the ball rolling.
And people always think, you know, you kind of sort of alluded to it yourself that mergers and acquisitions is this mysterious thing.
And that's why I'm here, to sort of try and break the mold for everybody.
Because it's not about investment bankers and lawyers and accountants and spreadsheets.
It's actually about people.
It's a very much a people business.
And if you can start and run a business, you've got all the qualifications you need to acquire a business or merge with a business.
It's just filling a form out for the government and paying some cash, maybe.
But there's nothing more complicated than that.
It's just two people or more agreeing on a deal, you know, and that doesn't.
There is no gatekeepers for this.
If you're a business owner and you find another business owner that wants to do a deal, then that's basically it.
It's not more complicated.
Right on.
Well, thank you.
I appreciate the conversation today, Andy.
This has been super helpful.
Yeah, no, my pleasure, my pleasure.
Lovely to meet you and let's stay in touch.
I'll send that email over after this, and then you've got it.
That'd be great to hand.
All right.
Enjoy the rest of your day.
You too.

summary.overview: In the recent Business Development and Consultative Sales Call between Miles Marmo and Andy Day, Miles provided insights into his agency, Agency Squid, specialized in sectors like adult beverages and luxury goods, and shared his challenges in transitioning the business as he and his father consider retirement. Andy, representing Capital A, clarified their role as M&A advisors and discussed various pathways for Agency Squid’s growth, including potential acquisition or merger options that could dilute equity but offer complementary partnerships to ease Miles’ operational managerial focus. The meeting highlighted the importance of people in M&A and concluded with agreed action items, such as Andy sending more information about Capital A's services and Miles needing to discuss potential strategies with his father and explore local agencies for merger opportunities.
summary.short_summary: Miles Marmo from Agency Squid and Andy Day of Capital A engaged in a consultative sales call to explore growth strategies for Agency Squid, which specializes in adult beverages and luxury goods. With $1.5 million in revenue and a focus on operational management, Miles is considering his father's retirement and the future of the agency. Andy, representing Capital A as M&A advisors, discussed potential paths for growth, including acquisition and merger options that could dilute equity but provide complementary partnerships. Emphasizing the significance of people in M&A, the conversation highlighted the need for Miles to explore local merger opportunities and the importance of discussing strategies with his father. Action items included Andy sending more information about Capital A's services and Miles considering his succession plan.
